source_name: Slint 1.17.1 — Animations, States & Transitions, Rectangle reference, and core source
key_claims: Property animation is declared with `animate <prop> { duration; delay; iteration-count; easing; direction; enabled; }`; multiple props can share one animate block.

`duration` defaults to 0ms; `iteration-count` is a float where a negative value means infinite and fractional values are allowed; `animation-tick()` is provided for permanently-running / time-driven animation.

`easing` defaults to linear and accepts the named easings.net set PLUS `cubic-bezier(a,b,c,d)` (confirmed in source: EasingCurve::CubicBezier([f32;4])). There is NO spring easing variant (EasingCurve enum = Linear, CubicBezier, EaseIn/Out/InOut Elastic, EaseIn/Out/InOut Bounce only; Custom is commented out).
`direction` supports normal/reverse/alternate/alternate-reverse (CSS-equivalent) for loops.
`enabled: false` makes the property jump to its target instantly with no delay/easing/iteration — this is the documented reduced-motion hook.
States (`states [ name when <cond> : { props } ]`) plus `in {} / out {} / in-out {}` transition blocks bind `animate` to state changes — the Slint equivalent of CSS state-driven transitions.

Rectangle exposes background (brush, supports @linear-gradient), border-color, border-width, border-radius, clip — but NO CSS-style box-shadow and NO blur on the box. The render core has a separate `BoxShadow` primitive (offset-x/offset-y/color/blur/spread) confirmed in internal/core/items.rs.
There is NO backdrop-filter / live backdrop blur anywhere in the core (no `backdrop` symbol in internal/core/items.rs or graphics.rs).
Animatable per-element visual/transform properties (confirmed in internal/core/items.rs): opacity, visible, rotate (rotation-angle + origin), scale (+origin), translate, cache-rendering-hint.

PopupWindow (confirmed in internal/compiler/typeregister.rs) provides show()/close() functions and a `close-on-click` bool; it has NO built-in open/close animation, so entrance/exit must be driven by animating the popup root's opacity/scale/translate (and exit-then-close via a Timer).

easing: linear | named Penner set (quad/cubic/quart/quint/sine/expo/circ/back/elastic/bounce, in/in-out/out) | cubic-bezier(a,b,c,d)
NO spring easing; NO @keyframes; NO backdrop-filter; NO CSS box-shadow on Rectangle (separate BoxShadow primitive: offset-x, offset-y, color, blur, spread)

date_or_version: Media Queries Level 5; page last modified 2026-06-10
key_claims: prefers-reduced-motion detects a user OS setting to minimize non-essential motion; `reduce` evaluates true and `no-preference` false.
The motivation is vestibular motion disorders; scaling or panning large objects are named triggers.

The recommended pattern is to TONE DOWN or REPLACE motion, not merely delete it — the worked example swaps a scale `pulse` for an opacity-only `dissolve`, preserving the signal while removing the vestibular trigger.
OS hooks exist across platforms (macOS Reduce motion, Windows Animation Effects, GNOME/KDE animation settings), so a desktop app can/should read the system preference.

source_name: W3C WCAG 2.1 — Understanding SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions
key_claims: Motion animation triggered by interaction must be disable-able unless it is ESSENTIAL to the functionality or information conveyed.
Non-essential motion can trigger vestibular reactions (dizziness, nausea, migraine); parallax and scroll-driven movement are called out as common offenders.

Definition: 'motion animation' = adding steps between conditions to create the illusion of movement; changes of color or opacity that do NOT change perceived size/shape/position are lower risk (errata now includes blur as motion).
Three compliant strategies: avoid unnecessary animation; provide a user control to turn it off; honor the OS reduce-motion setting.
Sufficient techniques: C39 (CSS prefers-reduced-motion) and SCR40 (JS). Essential animation (e.g. the movement IS the content) is allowed.

source_name: NN/g — Response Times: The 3 Important Limits
date_or_version: Jakob Nielsen, 1993 (web update 2014); excerpt from Usability Engineering (1993)
key_claims: 0.1 second is the limit for the user to feel the system reacts instantaneously / for direct manipulation (no special feedback needed).
1.0 second is the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted; delays of 0.2-1.0s are noticed and the user loses the feeling of operating directly on the data.
10 seconds is the limit for keeping the user's attention; beyond it a percent-done indicator and a way to interrupt are required.
Animations must be timed by a real-time clock, not by CPU execution speed; a UI can be 'too fast' (display inertia — changes flashing too rapidly stress users).

source_name: Motion for React (Framer Motion) — Transitions docs
key_claims: A transition has type 'tween' | 'spring' | 'inertia'; tween default duration is 0.3s (0.8s for keyframes) with an ease that can be a named curve or a cubic-bezier array.

Springs are physics-based (stiffness/damping/mass) and incorporate the velocity of existing gestures for natural feedback; they can also be duration-based (duration + bounce) and generated as pure CSS.
Inertia decelerates a value by its initial velocity and can snap-to-grid via modifyTarget — the model used for drag release / settle.
MotionConfig manages default transitions AND reduced-motion preferences; orchestration via delay/stagger/delayChildren and when:beforeChildren/afterChildren.
visualDuration lets a spring's perceived settle time be coordinated with time-based animations.

source_name: GSAP — Easing reference (and Flip / Draggable / Inertia plugins)
key_claims: 'Easing is the primary way to change the timing of your tweens' — the ease carries the feel/personality of the motion.

Default ease is power1.out; the core provides power1-4 (quad/cubic/quart/quint), back, bounce, circ, elastic, expo, sine, steps, plus EasePack (rough/slow/expoScale) and CustomEase/CustomBounce/CustomWiggle.

source_name: Material Design 3 — Easing and duration tokens & specs
date_or_version: Material Design 3 (M3); note: GM3 Expressive now uses a spring physics system, easing+duration kept for transitions
key_claims: The expressive direction is a spring physics system; the easing+duration token system remains for transitions and for teams not yet on Expressive.
Emphasized easing (decelerate/accelerate) is the expressive workhorse; Standard easing is for small/utility transitions.
Durations are tiered by traversed area: short (small utility), medium (medium screen area), long (large expressive, paired with Emphasized), extra-long (ambient, no user input).
Reference pairings: selection control 200ms + Standard; FAB->Sheet 400ms + Emphasized; Card->full-screen 500ms + Emphasized; ambient carousel 1000ms.

Two motion styles: productive (efficient, subtle, task-focused: microinteractions, dropdowns, data tables/viz) and expressive (significant moments: opening a page, primary action, system alerts/notifications). Reserve expressive for occasional important moments.

'Strictly linear movement appears unnatural'; elements speed up quickly and slow down smoothly (light-weight material). 'Do not use easing curves that suggest bounce, stretch, or sudden stops.' Avoid purely decorative easing.
Exit easing speeds up to imply permanent departure; EXCEPTION: an element that leaves but stays nearby (e.g. a side panel) uses standard easing so it feels recallable.
Micro-interactions use ease-out on user input and fall in a 90-120ms static band. Duration scales non-linearly with distance/size of change.
'The best interface motion may go unnoticed.' Always provide static alternatives; consider reduced motion for mobile/tablet.

Choreography: motion paths follow the grid and never run diagonally — stagger horizontal+vertical to make rounded-corner paths; criss-cross sorting 'appears disorganized — avoid'. Semantic/spatial/intentional consistency. Higher layer = slide + dim-below; same layer = push/mask. Continuity via shared elements that 'should not distract'. Stagger table rows ~20ms, keep total < 500ms. Sequence: shell -> body -> dynamic content -> primary action -> data viz.

date_or_version: Apple HIG; updated 2025-09-09 (incl. Liquid Glass guidance)
key_claims: 'Add motion purposefully... Don't add motion for the sake of adding motion. Gratuitous or excessive animation can distract people and may make them feel disconnected or physically uncomfortable.'
'Make motion optional' — never use motion as the only way to communicate important information; supplement with haptics/audio.
Feedback motion should be realistic and follow gestures/expectations; a mismatched dismiss direction (reveal down, dismiss sideways) disorients.
'Aim for brevity and precision' — brief, precise feedback often conveys information more effectively than prominent animation.
'Avoid adding motion to UI interactions that occur frequently.'
'Let people cancel motion' — don't make users wait for an animation to complete, especially repeated ones (supports interruptible/reversible motion).

Maintain 30-60fps; avoid peripheral/edge motion and sustained ~0.2Hz oscillation (vestibular); use fades to relocate objects whose movement communicates nothing; SwiftUI applies built-in in/out easing that cannot be customized.

key_claims: Principles: Purposeful (surface connections between states/views, draw attention, give feedback), Intuitive (mirrors real-world acceleration/gravity/volume), Seamless ('just enough to get the intention across and no more'; 'never slow them down').
Three easings: ease-out for fading/animating INTO view (most common), ease-in for exiting/fading out, ease-in-out for place-to-place movement (draws attention; reserve for bigger movements).

Duration considers element complexity, easing, and scale; micro animations cover small ground (color fades, hovers, accordions, tooltips), macro animations cover large ground (panel/drawer reveals, cross-screen movement).
Don't build custom components solely to follow animation guidelines — prefer native controls to leverage built-in accessibility.
react-spring models motion as a physics spring (tension/friction, mass defaults to 1) via an `animated` primitive and useSpring.
It ships named config presets that map intent to tension/friction pairs — an inspectable, widely-reused reference for 'how stiff/damped should a UI spring feel'.

These preset values are the same family the PM prototypes already use in their JS spring knobs (e.g. basic ~ stiffness 210 / damping 26), confirming the prototype's spring feel is react-spring-derived.

org: Tversky, Morrison & Betrancourt (academic, Int. J. Human-Computer Studies)
key_claims: Animation's apparent superiority over static graphics usually comes from extra information or interactivity, not from motion itself (i.e. motion alone is not a comprehension win).
Apprehension Principle: animation must be apprehensible — viewers must be able to perceive and make sense of it; too-fast or too-complex animation fails.
Expressive Principle: animation should express the change/message so viewers can infer the meaning.

Animation helps when it externalizes a change in spatial structure over time (a route, a mechanism, a state transition); decorative or poorly-designed animation does not aid, and can impede, comprehension.

org: Simons & Levin (academic, Trends in Cognitive Sciences)
key_claims: Observers frequently fail to detect large changes in a visual scene, especially when the change coincides with a visual disruption (a cut, flicker, saccade, or repaint).
Attention is required to perceive change; without a continuity cue, object identity is lost across the disruption.

Implication for UI: if an element is removed and re-added (or jumps) with no continuous transformation, users may not connect the before/after states — continuous motion (FLIP/connected animation) preserves object identity and spatial understanding.
